import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

Desktop apps, CLIs and developer tools sign users in through the Seamless Auth
[OpenID Provider](/build/openid-provider) as **public clients**, following RFC 8252 (OAuth 2.0 for
Native Apps). The app opens the user's system browser on the hosted sign-in page, the user signs in
there (with a passkey or any other enabled method), and the browser hands an authorization code back
to the app through a loopback address or a private-use URI scheme. The app exchanges the code with
PKCE. It never sees the user's credentials and never holds a client secret.

Read [Use Seamless Auth As An OpenID Provider](/build/openid-provider) first for the edge service,
the registry and the token model. This page covers what is different for native apps.

<Aside type="note" title="Status">
  Ships in v0.21 with the OpenID Provider. Native sign-out and the device authorization grant (for
  CLIs on machines without a browser) are still being built. Their sections below are placeholders.
</Aside>

---

## The Rules

1. **Register a public client.** A native app cannot keep a secret: anything in the binary can be
   extracted. A public client authenticates with PKCE alone, has no secret and no keys, and cannot
   use `client_credentials`. The registry refuses any other combination.
2. **Use the system browser, never an embedded webview.** A webview lets the app read what the user
   types, and the user cannot tell a real sign-in page from a copy. Open the authorization URL in the
   default browser (or `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on macOS and iOS, Custom Tabs on Android).
3. **Use PKCE with `S256`.** Every client must. The edge refuses `plain` and requests without PKCE.
4. **Receive the code on a loopback redirect or a private-use scheme.** See the next section.
5. **Keep tokens in the OS credential store**: the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the
   Secret Service API (GNOME Keyring, KWallet) on Linux. Not a plain file, not an environment
   variable.

---

## Redirect URIs

A public client registers its redirect URIs like any other application. The registry and the edge
accept three forms:

| Form                | Example                       | Matching                                                                   |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| IPv4 loopback       | `http://127.0.0.1/callback`   | Any port at request time. Scheme, host and path must match exactly.       |
| IPv6 loopback       | `http://[::1]/callback`       | Any port at request time. Scheme, host and path must match exactly.       |
| Private-use scheme  | `com.example.desk:/callback`  | Exact. The scheme must be in reverse domain form.                          |
| Claimed `https` URL | `https://desk.example.com/cb` | Exact, port included. For apps that claim links (universal or app links). |

An application with a loopback or private-use redirect is reported as `applicationType: native`.

### Loopback on any port (RFC 8252 section 7.3)

Register the loopback URI **without a port**. At sign-in, the app listens on whatever port the OS
gives it and sends that port in `redirect_uri`:

```text
registered:   http://127.0.0.1/callback
requested:    http://127.0.0.1:53124/callback     accepted
requested:    http://[::1]:61000/callback         accepted if http://[::1]/callback is registered
requested:    http://127.0.0.1:53124/other        refused (path differs)
requested:    https://127.0.0.1:53124/callback    refused (scheme differs)
requested:    http://127.0.0.2:53124/callback     refused (host differs)
requested:    http://localhost:53124/callback     refused (localhost)
```

Bind the listener to the loopback interface only (`127.0.0.1` or `::1`), never to all interfaces.
The port exception applies only to these loopback URIs. A web application's `https` redirect never
matches on a different port.

### Why not `localhost`

`localhost` is refused as a redirect host, at registration and at sign-in (RFC 8252 section 8.3).
The name can resolve to an address other than the loopback interface, or to the IPv6 address when
the app listens on IPv4. Use the literal `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`.

### Private-use schemes (RFC 8252 section 7.1)

A private-use scheme must be in reverse domain form, a name with at least one dot that you control,
such as `com.example.desk:/callback`. The dot keeps out `javascript:`, `data:` and every other scheme
a browser acts on. Register the scheme with the OS so the browser hands the redirect to your app.
Any app can claim the same scheme on most platforms, which is why PKCE is required: an app that
intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier.

## A CLI Example

A complete loopback sign-in for a Node CLI, with [`openid-client`](https://github.com/panva/openid-client).
Register the client first:

```bash
seamless clients create "Example CLI" --public --first-party \
  --redirect-uri http://127.0.0.1/callback \
  --grants authorization_code,refresh_token
```

```ts
import { createServer } from 'node:http'
import { once } from 'node:events'
import open from 'open'
import * as oidc from 'openid-client'

const config = await oidc.discovery(
  new URL('https://login.example.com'),
  'CLI_CLIENT_ID',
  undefined,
  oidc.None(),
)

// Port 0: the OS picks a free port on the loopback interface.
const server = createServer()
server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')
await once(server, 'listening')
const { port } = server.address() as { port: number }
const redirectUri = `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/callback`

const verifier = oidc.randomPKCECodeVerifier()
const state = oidc.randomState()
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: redirectUri,
  scope: 'openid offline_access',
  prompt: 'consent',
  code_challenge: await oidc.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(verifier),
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
  state,
})

await open(url.href)

const [request, response] = await once(server, 'request')
const callbackUrl = new URL(request.url, redirectUri)
response.end('Signed in. You can close this tab.')
server.close()

const tokens = await oidc.authorizationCodeGrant(config, callbackUrl, {
  pkceCodeVerifier: verifier,
  expectedState: state,
})
// Store tokens.refresh_token in the OS credential store.
```

`offline_access` with `prompt=consent` gets a refresh token, so the CLI does not send the user back
to the browser every time the access token expires. See [Refresh tokens](/build/openid-provider#refresh-tokens).

---

## Refresh, API Tokens And Sign-Out

- **Refresh.** Refresh tokens rotate on every use. Save the new one each time, before using the new
  access token. A refresh token used twice revokes the grant and ends the user's Seamless session,
  so two processes of the same app must not refresh with one token at the same time.
- **Tokens for your API.** Ask for a token for a named API with `resource=<identifier>` on the
  authorization request, using a resource the application is linked to. The access token is an RFC
  9068 JWT whose `aud` is that API. See
  [Access tokens for your API](/build/openid-provider#access-tokens-for-your-api).
- **Signing out of the app.** Revoke the refresh token at `/token/revocation` (a public client sends
  its `client_id`), then delete the stored tokens. That ends this app's grant only. The user stays
  signed in to Seamless in the browser and in their other apps.

<Aside type="note" title="In progress: full sign-out">
  Ending the user's Seamless session from a native app (RP-initiated logout through the system
  browser) is being built in
  [seamless-auth-oidc-provider#5](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/issues/5).
  This section will cover it once it ships.
</Aside>

## CLIs Without A Browser: Device Authorization Grant

<Aside type="note" title="In progress">
  The device authorization grant (RFC 8628), for a CLI on a server or container with no browser, is
  being built in
  [seamless-auth-oidc-provider#7](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/issues/7).
  It will be available to first-party applications with `deviceFlowEnabled`. This section will cover
  the flow once it ships. Until then, a CLI needs a machine with a browser for the loopback flow.

## Why Passkeys Run On The Hosted Page

A passkey is bound to a relying party ID, the instance's `rpid` (for example `example.com`), and a
browser only offers it on a page whose origin is that domain or a subdomain of it. The hosted
sign-in page runs on the provider's issuer (for example `https://login.example.com`), which the API
requires to sit under `rpid`, so every passkey the user already has works there.

An app's own webview cannot do the same. Its origin is `tauri://localhost`, `app://`, `file://` or
similar, which can never match `rpid`, so the WebAuthn ceremony fails, and an embedded webview
cannot reach the passkeys synced to the user's browser or phone in any case. Sending the user to
the system browser keeps passkeys, saved sessions and any security keys working, and keeps the app
out of the credential path.

---

## What OAuth 2.1 Refuses

The provider is locked to OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9700. These are refused for every client, native or
not:

| Refused                                                       | Answer                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Implicit and hybrid flows (`response_type=token`, `id_token`) | `unsupported_response_type` or `invalid_request`          |
| PKCE `plain`, or no PKCE                                      | `invalid_request`                                         |
| Resource owner password grant (`grant_type=password`)         | `unsupported_grant_type`                                  |
| A redirect URI that does not match a registered one           | An error page; the code is never sent there               |
| `localhost` or a non-loopback `http` redirect                 | Refused at registration and at sign-in                    |
| A client secret on a public client                            | Refused at registration                                   |
| `client_credentials` for a public client                      | Refused at registration                                   |
| An authorization code redeemed twice                          | `invalid_grant`, and the tokens from the first use are revoked |
| Dynamic client registration                                   | Not offered: applications come only from the registry     |
